name: SpaceX reusable launch stack
description: SpaceX-centered reusable orbital launch capability map. Falcon 9 and Starship/Super Heavy are separated as product branches; Dragon, Starlink service, Falcon Heavy, and payload customer products are intentionally excluded from the product boundary.

targetContext.targetScale: repeatable orbital launch and recovery across Falcon 9 operations plus Starship/Super Heavy development
targetContext.targetPerformance: launch cadence, booster reuse, safe recovery, rapid refurbishment, payload mass-to-orbit, and cost-per-kg reduction
targetContext.targetUseCase: commercial, government, and internal SpaceX orbital logistics
targetContext.targetEnvironment: US launch/reentry licensing, ocean/RTLS recovery operations, and high-cadence launch sites

name: Reusable orbital launch capability
description: Demand-side capability: move payload mass to orbit with reusable launch hardware, high cadence, controlled recovery, and bounded refurbishment cost.

name: Falcon 9 reusable branch
description: Operational Falcon 9 reuse route centered on first-stage recovery, Merlin reuse, fault-tolerant avionics, fairing recovery, and post-flight refurbishment. It is commercially mature, but the investable constraint is how much inspection, acceptance testing, range availability, and mission propellant reserve still gate cadence and marginal cost.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources support Falcon 9 reuse and mission examples, but not an audited reusable-branch cost per flight, refurbishment cost, recovery cost, or incremental margin from an extra reflight.

name: Starship / Super Heavy reusable branch
description: Development route for a fully reusable Starship upper stage and reusable Super Heavy booster, with much larger payload capacity but unresolved rapid-reuse, heat-shield, tower-catch, and licensing constraints.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support route status and regulatory cadence context, but not Starship/Super Heavy reuse cost per flight, refurbishment cost, or mature launch price.

name: Common reuse enablers
description: Shared reuse layer across SpaceX vehicles: health monitoring, engine life margin, flight safety, propellant operations, acceptance testing, and recovery operations.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support SpaceX reuse operations, but not a separated cost for health monitoring, inspection, acceptance testing, recovery operations, and reuse margin across vehicles.

name: Launch and ground operations stack
description: Ground-side infrastructure and process layer for high-cadence reusable launch: tower systems, propellant loading, pad turnaround, static-fire acceptance, and range coordination.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support ground-cadence and licensing constraints, but not the audited cost of pad, tower, propellant, range, and turnaround capacity.

name: Falcon 9 booster reuse stack
description: First-stage branch covering booster propulsion, structure, reentry control, landing hardware, recovery operations, and refurbishment. It matters because every relaunch must clear recovered-stage inspection and acceptance confidence before cadence can translate into lower marginal launch cost.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources identify reusable first-stage hardware, but not the audited booster inspection, replacement, transport, and acceptance-test cost per reflight.

name: Falcon 9 Merlin engine cluster
description: Nine-engine Merlin first-stage propulsion cluster; reuse economics depend on engine life margin, inspection time, and acceptance test yield.

name: Merlin reuse qualification
description: Reuse acceptance logic for engine inspections, trend data, hot-fire margins, and flight readiness after recovery. It is a bottleneck because a conservative engine screen protects reliability but can force extra test time, part replacement, or booster retirement before the market sees the true marginal cost of reuse.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source separates Merlin reuse qualification labor, instrumentation, replacement scope, or hot-fire acceptance cost from whole-launch economics.

name: Merlin turbopump reuse inspection
description: Inspection and trend-screening of turbomachinery after recovery. It is hard to clear quickly because turbopump life is driven by high-speed rotating hardware, thermal cycling, and anomaly history, while public details remain thin enough that this branch must stay a research frontier.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources do not price non-destructive inspection, teardown thresholds, replaced turbomachinery parts, or acceptance-test impact for recovered Merlin engines.

name: Merlin chamber and nozzle life margin
description: Thermal and structural life-margin model for repeated engine starts, ascent load, entry burn, and landing burn. The constraint is not whether the engine can fly once; it is how confidently SpaceX can extend reuse life without expensive inspection or early retirement.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices chamber/nozzle life margin, replacement thresholds, or the cost of adding reuse cycles through materials and acceptance testing.

name: Falcon 9 aluminum-lithium tank structure
description: Reusable stage structure and tank system; repeated loads and landing environments make structural inspection and fatigue margin relevant.

name: Falcon 9 stage fatigue life
description: Fatigue tracking for recovered stages across ascent, reentry, landing, transport, and relaunch cycles. It gates reuse depth because the operator must prove structural margin without turning every recovery into a slow teardown campaign.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources do not provide an audited fatigue-life model, inspection-hour count, replacement threshold, or per-cycle structural margin cost.

name: Falcon 9 grid-fin reentry control
description: Deployable grid fins used to steer the returning booster during atmospheric reentry toward a landing zone or droneship.

name: Falcon 9 landing legs
description: Deployable first-stage landing legs for vertical recovery; a mature subsystem but still part of the recovery reliability chain.

name: Falcon 9 boostback, entry, and landing burns
description: Guidance and propellant allocation across recovery burns; directly controls recovery success and payload performance tradeoffs.

name: Falcon 9 landing propellant margin
description: Mission-design tradeoff between payload delivery and reserve propellant for boostback, entry, and landing burns. It is a capacity/economics bottleneck because higher recovery reserve can protect hardware but reduce payload margin or force droneship profiles.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices the payload opportunity cost of recovery propellant, droneship use, or mission-specific reserve policy.

name: Falcon 9 droneship / RTLS recovery ops
description: Operational workflow for autonomous spaceport droneship or return-to-launch-site recovery, safing, transport, and reuse handoff. It can bottleneck launch cadence when sea-state, ship availability, port logistics, or landing-site availability break the recovery-to-refurbishment chain.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources do not provide an audited droneship/RTLS operations cost, recovery-cycle time, or weather/port-capacity loss rate.

name: Falcon 9 post-flight inspection and refurbishment
description: Turnaround process after booster recovery; bottleneck is time, inspection confidence, replacement scope, and acceptance testing before reflight. This is the most direct Falcon 9 reuse constraint because it converts recovered hardware into sellable launch capacity.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices post-flight inspection labor, acceptance-test hours, refurbishment material, or queue time per recovered booster.

name: Falcon 9 second-stage payload delivery
description: Expendable upper-stage delivery layer. It is not the reusable hardware itself, but it affects Falcon 9 mission envelope and launch economics.

name: Merlin Vacuum upper-stage engine
description: Single Merlin Vacuum engine on Falcon upper stage; payload guide notes the fixed nozzle and upper-stage role.

name: Falcon 9 fault-tolerant avionics and GNC
description: Fault-tolerant avionics and guidance, navigation, and control layer with single-fault tolerance and redundant/triplicated elements according to the payload guide. It is commercially mature, but reuse still depends on flight-software confidence, sensor redundancy, anomaly review, and recovery guidance reliability.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: The Falcon payload guide supports avionics architecture context, but not the audited cost of fault-tolerant GNC software, redundancy, post-flight data review, or recovery guidance qualification.

name: Falcon 9 pneumatic stage separation
description: Low-shock separation subsystem documented in the Falcon payload guide; important because separation reliability affects mission and reuse safety.

name: Falcon 9 fairing recovery and reuse
description: Payload-fairing recovery and reuse branch; economically relevant but separate from first-stage reuse.

name: Starship / Super Heavy vehicle stack
description: Integrated booster and ship architecture for the Starship route. It bottlenecks commercialization because full reuse needs the booster, ship, heat shield, propellant operations, tower interface, and licensing cadence to work as one repeatable system rather than isolated test successes.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources support the architecture and route status, but not audited Starship/Super Heavy reuse cost per flight, turnaround cost, or mature launch cadence economics.

name: Super Heavy reusable booster
description: Reusable first-stage booster branch for Starship/Super Heavy, including Raptor cluster, boostback, grid fins, and catch interface. It is constrained by engine-cluster reliability, RTLS guidance, tower catch margin, and ground-site uptime, so recovery success alone is not enough for high-cadence commercial reuse.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources do not price Super Heavy booster refurbishment, tower-catch inspection, Raptor reuse margin, or recovery operations per flight.

name: Super Heavy 33-Raptor engine cluster
description: Large clustered methalox propulsion layer for Super Heavy; a key integration bottleneck for reliability, throttling, and reuse.

name: Raptor methalox staged-combustion engine
description: Reusable methane/oxygen engine family used on Starship and Super Heavy; engine reliability and reuse margin are central to the route.

name: Raptor clean reuse margin
description: Engine-health and combustion-stability margin needed for repeated launch, landing, and relaunch cycles.

name: Subcooled methane / oxygen propellant ops
description: Ground loading, densification, boiloff control, and engine feed operations for subcooled liquid methane and oxygen.

name: Super Heavy grid-fin control
description: Grid-fin and control-surface layer for Super Heavy return and catch profiles.

name: Super Heavy tower-catch interface
description: Launch tower catch interface. This is a high-leverage Starship reuse bottleneck because it replaces landing legs with site-specific infrastructure, precision approach logic, site availability, and post-catch inspection capacity.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: FAA materials support tower/cadence context, but no reviewed source prices tower catch hardware, site downtime, inspection throughput, or catch-related refurbishment.

name: Super Heavy RTLS boostback profile
description: Return-to-launch-site mission design and control method for Super Heavy recovery. It bottlenecks Starship cadence because propellant reserve, landing accuracy, abort envelopes, and tower availability must line up without sacrificing payload economics.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices the payload opportunity cost, guidance reserve, abort margin, or site-turnaround impact of Super Heavy RTLS recovery.

name: Starship reusable ship upper stage
description: Reusable upper-stage/spacecraft branch for orbital delivery and return. It is the hardest route element because orbital reentry, heat-shield durability, flap control, engine relight, payload bay operations, and post-flight inspection all have to converge into repeatable reuse.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public sources support Starship reuse intent, but no reviewed source prices upper-stage refurbishment, heat-shield replacement, reentry recovery margin, or mature ship turnaround.

name: Starship sea-level and vacuum Raptor mix
description: Ship propulsion mix of sea-level and vacuum-optimized Raptor engines, per 2026 filing descriptions.

name: Starship heat-shield tile system
description: Reusable thermal-protection layer for ship reentry; tile durability, attachment, inspection, and replacement time are central bottlenecks. It directly controls whether Starship reuse looks like aircraft-style turnaround or like a slow refurbishment campaign.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices heat-shield tile replacement, inspection hours, bonding yield, reentry damage rate, or reuse-cycle life.

name: Starship tile bonding and inspection process
description: Tile attachment, gap control, inspection, replacement, and reflight acceptance process after ascent vibration, heating, and reentry cycles. This is a bottleneck because rapid Starship reuse depends on finding damaged tiles, restoring bond and gap integrity, and clearing the ship for another flight without turning every recovery into a slow thermal-protection refurbishment campaign.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices Starship tile bonding labor, inspection hours, replacement rate, gap-filler acceptance, bond-yield learning, or reflight qualification. Cost evidence needs a Starship-specific turnaround workflow, not a generic tile material price.

name: Starship stainless-steel primary structure
description: Stainless-steel structure selected for Starship-class thermal and manufacturing tradeoffs; exact alloy/process details remain outside this first pass.

name: Starship flap reentry control
description: Ship flaps and control method for atmospheric reentry, attitude control, and landing transition.

name: Starship orbital payload deployment bay
description: Payload accommodation and deployment branch for high-mass Starship missions.

name: Starship reentry and landing burn profile
description: Flight-control method for ship reentry, flip, engine relight, and terminal landing burn. It bottlenecks reuse because reentry control, thermal margin, relight reliability, landing accuracy, and post-flight condition all determine whether the ship can be reflown at commercial cadence.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices ship reentry guidance margin, landing-burn reserve, relight failure reserve, or post-landing acceptance cost.

name: Integrated launch tower and chopsticks
description: Launch, stacking, and catch infrastructure for Starship/Super Heavy; makes reuse dependent on ground-site precision and uptime.

name: Methane / oxygen ground propellant system
description: Storage, loading, chilldown, and tank farm operations for high-cadence methalox launch.

name: Launch-pad rapid turnaround process
description: Pad inspection, repair, propellant reset, range readiness, and vehicle integration process between launches.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Public FAA review supports site cadence context, but no reviewed source prices pad repair, propellant reset, range readiness, and vehicle-integration turnaround per launch.

name: Vehicle health monitoring telemetry
description: Flight and ground telemetry pipeline used to decide whether recovered hardware can fly again.

name: Reuse acceptance and static-fire process
description: Test and acceptance workflow after assembly or refurbishment, including static-fire logic where required.

name: Autonomous flight safety system
description: Flight safety system layer that bounds public-safety risk during launch and recovery operations.

name: Range safety and airspace coordination
description: Coordination of hazard areas, launch windows, NOTAMs, range assets, and recovery zones for high-cadence operations.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: The binding constraint is external scheduling and safety coordination; reviewed public sources do not provide a separable cost per additional launch window or range event.

name: Cryogenic ground loading sequence
description: Sequencing, chilldown, propellant conditioning, hold logic, and abort recovery for cryogenic launch operations.

name: Methalox engine test stands
description: Ground test infrastructure for Raptor qualification, acceptance, anomaly reproduction, and reuse margin learning.

name: FAA launch and reentry cadence license
description: Regulatory cadence constraint for SpaceX launch and reentry activity. For Starship/Super Heavy Boca Chica, the FAA page references proposed authorization for up to 25 annual orbital launches and landings.

name: Reusable launch cost per kg
description: Investor-facing metric for whether reuse translates into payload-mass economics, not just recovery spectacle. The current graph keeps this as a blocking unknown until launch price, payload mass, reuse depth, refurbishment, and recovery cost are tied to reviewed sources.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: Blocking commercial unknown: public route evidence does not yet support a reviewed cost-per-kg value separated by Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, Starship, payload class, reuse depth, and refurbishment scope.

name: Booster reflight count
description: Observed booster reuse depth; SpaceX 2026 filing language is evidence for high repeat use but still requires independent operational audit before it can drive cost claims.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: Needs a reviewed fleet-level source that links booster serials, flight counts, retirement causes, refurbishment cycles, and mission class before it can support investment conclusions.

name: Launch cadence
description: Cadence metric linking vehicle reuse, pad turnaround, regulatory approval, and demand backlog. It is useful only when split by site and vehicle route because FAA/site authorization, ground operations, recovery assets, and customer demand can bind separately.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: FAA materials support site-specific review context, but the graph still needs a reviewed cadence series by vehicle, launch site, landing mode, and license scope.

name: SpaceX orbital data center system
description: SpaceX-centered research map for an orbital AI compute / data-center system. Public evidence supports an FCC application and investor-facing intent, but not a mature commercial service; the central question is whether power, heat rejection, radiation resilience, launch cadence, and useful compute economics can clear at the same time.

targetContext.targetScale: large NGSO constellation of compute satellites if authorized and economically feasible
targetContext.targetPerformance: compute power in orbit, thermal rejection, optical backhaul, radiation resilience, safe constellation operations, and launch cost per useful kW
targetContext.targetUseCase: AI training/inference and data-center workloads using orbital solar power and Starlink-style optical networking
targetContext.targetEnvironment: LEO/NGSO orbital shells, FCC/space-debris constraints, high-radiation/high-vacuum thermal environment

metrics.name: Commercial readiness
metrics.description: Reviewed FCC evidence supports application scope, not approval, deployment, service launch, useful compute capacity, revenue, or economics.

metrics.name: Core pricing gap
metrics.description: No reviewed public source yet ties useful compute kW, payload lifetime, power/thermal throttling, launch cost, replacement cadence, and utilization into a cost per useful compute kW.

name: Orbital AI compute capability
description: Demand-side capability: deliver useful AI compute from orbit with reliable power, cooling, communication, fault tolerance, and regulatory compliance.

name: Orbital compute payload stack
description: Compute payload branch: accelerators, memory, storage, management, redundancy, software orchestration, and radiation/fault mitigation.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources do not price orbital accelerator racks, memory, storage, radiation recovery, power derating, and qualification as an audited compute-payload stack.

name: Orbital AI accelerator payload racks
description: High-power accelerator payload hardware adapted for launch loads, vacuum, radiation, power cycling, and remote operation. It is a bottleneck because dense AI hardware assumes terrestrial cooling, maintenance, and replacement access, while an orbital rack must survive qualification and operate within strict power/thermal limits.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices space-adapted accelerator racks, launch-qualified packaging, derating, radiation mitigation, spares, or useful compute loss from throttling.

name: Radiation-tolerant compute board
description: Board-level compute design with shielding, redundancy, power integrity, thermal conduction, and fault recovery. The bottleneck is reconciling high-performance commercial silicon with total-dose and single-event-effect risk without destroying useful compute density.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed radiation sources explain the hazard, but no reviewed source prices board-level shielding, derating, redundancy, watchdog recovery, or qualified compute throughput.

name: GPU / CPU payload qualification
description: Screening, burn-in, thermal-vacuum, radiation, and fault-injection qualification for high-power AI compute payloads. It is a bottleneck because each hardware generation changes faster than traditional space qualification cycles, so useful deployed capacity can lag terrestrial accelerator availability.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices qualification cycles, lot screening, burn-in yield, or launch-ready payload acceptance for GPU/CPU compute racks.

name: Fault-tolerant orbital job orchestration
description: Distributed scheduler and recovery method for compute jobs under node resets, radiation upsets, link outages, and orbital handoffs.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support space-radiation fault modes, but there is no reviewed public pricing for an orbital compute scheduler, recovery software, utilization loss, or SLA reserve.

name: Orbital ECC memory and storage
description: Memory/storage branch for radiation-induced bit errors, restart recovery, local caching, and data integrity.

name: Onboard secure management plane
description: Remote update, key management, workload isolation, telemetry, and recovery controls for an unmanned orbital data center.

name: Orbital AI workload partitioning
description: Method for splitting training/inference workloads across intermittently connected orbital nodes with bounded latency and failure recovery.

name: Orbital compute firmware update process
description: Remote firmware/driver update, rollback, and recovery workflow for compute payloads that cannot be physically serviced often.

name: Spacecraft bus platform for compute
description: Satellite bus layer providing structure, power, thermal interfaces, attitude control, communications, propulsion, and operations services for compute payloads.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support spacecraft-bus functions, but not a compute-optimized bus price including power, thermal, attitude, propulsion, communications, and operations services.

name: Deployable solar power system
description: Solar-array branch for orbital compute power generation. High useful compute kW requires large deployed area, pointing, degradation management, and packaging.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources identify orbital power needs, but no reviewed source prices large deployable solar arrays, pointing, degradation margin, and packaging for orbital compute.

name: High-power solar array packaging
description: Packaging and deployment hardware for large solar arrays compatible with launch volume, loads, and high-volume satellite production. It bottlenecks useful compute because deployed power area, stowed volume, pointing, degradation, and factory yield all constrain how much payload power reaches accelerators.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources do not price compute-scale solar-array packaging, deployment mechanisms, pointing margin, degradation reserve, or high-volume array production.

name: Battery storage and power conditioning
description: Energy storage and conditioning layer for eclipse operations, peak compute loads, battery life, and power quality.

name: Rad-hard power distribution unit
description: Power distribution and protection electronics for high-power payloads in a radiation environment.

name: Eclipse power budget management
description: Scheduling and throttling method for orbital day/night cycles, battery state, thermal limits, and link availability.

name: Orbital energy-aware scheduler
description: Compute scheduler that turns orbital power/thermal states into workload placement and throttling decisions.

name: Orbital thermal rejection stack
description: Thermal branch for removing high compute heat in vacuum. This is the clearest first-order bottleneck because waste heat can only be moved and radiated, not convected away.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed thermal-control sources explain the physics bottleneck, but no reviewed source prices deployable radiators, cold plates, loops, coatings, throttling margin, and qualification for orbital AI compute.

name: Deployable radiator panels
description: Deployable radiators for high-power heat rejection; radiator area, deployment reliability, pointing, and degradation set useful compute density. The constraint is physical: in vacuum the heat must ultimately be radiated away, so compute density can be capped before silicon supply becomes the limiting factor.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: NASA thermal sources explain deployable radiator and heat-rejection logic, but no reviewed source prices radiator area, deployment reliability, coatings, qualification, or throttling reserve for orbital AI compute.

name: Heat-pipe / loop-heat-pipe network
description: Heat transport layer from accelerator payloads to radiator surfaces; failure modes include dryout, interface resistance, deployment motion, and thermal cycling.

name: Compute cold plate and fluid loop
description: Cold plates or fluid-loop elements that collect heat from dense accelerator payloads and move it toward radiators. It is a bottleneck because leak-free heat transport, pump reliability, interface resistance, and freeze/thaw behavior must be qualified without routine physical service.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices compute cold plates, working fluid loops, pump redundancy, leak testing, or qualification for high-power orbital payloads.

name: Radiator surface coatings and degradation
description: Radiator optical coatings and surface materials whose absorptivity/emissivity change under UV, atomic oxygen, and particle exposure.

name: Thermal modeling and control algorithm
description: Model predictive thermal control tying payload throttling, radiator attitude, orbital heating, and fault states together.

name: Optical ISL network fabric
description: High-bandwidth optical inter-satellite link network layer for compute satellites; FCC notice says the proposed system would primarily rely on optical ISLs and connect with Starlink systems.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources support optical inter-satellite link use, but not the audited cost of compute-grade optical crosslinks, routing, capacity reservation, and gateway integration.

name: Starlink laser-terminal backhaul
description: Laser-terminal and optical-backhaul layer; relevant because the FCC notice ties the data-center system to SpaceX first- and second-generation Starlink systems.

name: Optical pointing, acquisition, and tracking
description: PAT control required to keep high-rate laser links aligned across moving spacecraft.

name: Mesh routing and congestion control
description: Routing and load-balancing method for orbital mesh traffic between compute nodes, Starlink links, and ground gateways.

name: TT&C and ground-link layer
description: Telemetry, tracking, command, and ground-link operations layer; FCC notice identifies TT&C operations in the proposed system.

name: Starlink interconnect gateway
description: Gateway layer connecting orbital compute traffic to Starlink's broader network and ground users where authorized.

name: Radiation environment mitigation
description: Mitigation branch for total ionizing dose, single-event effects, solar activity, shielding, parts selection, and software recovery.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed radiation sources identify TID and single-event-effect hazards, but not a compute-constellation cost for shielding, part screening, redundancy, watchdog recovery, and lost utilization.

name: TID shielding and layout
description: Shielding, layout, and material strategy to keep electronics within mission radiation limits.

name: SEE watchdog and recovery
description: Detection and recovery for single-event upset/latchup/fault states affecting compute and power electronics.

name: COTS part screening and upscreening
description: Part selection, screening, derating, and lot control for non-traditional high-performance compute electronics in space. It bottlenecks scale because COTS accelerators and boards may be available commercially, but lot control, radiation screening, and derating can become the slow qualification path.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed source prices lot screening, radiation upscreening, derating loss, rejected lots, or replacement cadence for COTS compute parts in orbital data centers.

name: Orbital deployment launch stack
description: Launch and deployment branch for compute satellites: upmass, payload integration, deployment interfaces, orbital shell insertion, and cadence. It bottlenecks the product because useful compute economics depend on launch cadence, replacement cadence, payload integration, and regulatory clearance, not only on in-orbit hardware design.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources establish launch and deployment dependence, but not the audited launch, deployment interface, orbit-insertion cadence, and replacement-cadence cost for compute satellites.

name: Starship mass-to-orbit enabler
description: Heavy-lift economic enabler for orbital compute deployment; this is a dependency, not the data-center product itself. It is a bottleneck because orbital compute economics likely require cheap, high-cadence mass-to-orbit that is not yet a mature audited service at the assumed scale.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: SpaceX public material supports Starship heavy-lift intent, but not an audited launch cost per useful orbital compute kW or replacement-cadence cost.

name: Compute-satellite deployment interface
description: Mechanical/electrical launch accommodation and separation interface for large compute satellites.

name: Orbital shell constellation operations
description: Fleet operations for many compute satellites across orbital shells, handoffs, health checks, and capacity management.

name: Collision avoidance and deorbit compliance
description: Autonomous conjunction screening, maneuver planning, end-of-life disposal, and debris-risk management for a large NGSO compute constellation.

name: Space environment regulatory license
description: Authorization and waiver layer for SpaceX's proposed Orbital Data Center system; currently public-notice stage, not commercial deployment.

name: Manufacturing and qualification stack
description: Factory, test, and qualification branch for high-volume compute satellites.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources do not price the combined compute-satellite factory, thermal-vacuum, radiation, vibration, yield, and qualification throughput stack.

name: Thermal-vacuum test campaign
description: TVAC test process for compute payload, power, thermal rejection, and software throttling across mission thermal states.

name: Radiation test campaign
description: Test campaign for TID, SEE, latchup, reset behavior, and data integrity under expected orbit environment.

name: Vibration and launch-load test
description: Mechanical test branch for high-mass/high-power compute payloads and deployable power/thermal hardware.

name: High-volume compute satellite factory line
description: Factory process for producing compute satellites at meaningful scale; public evidence is currently too thin for capacity claims.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: The FCC notice establishes the proposed system scope, but no reviewed public source prices compute-satellite factory tooling, test throughput, yield, or qualified monthly output.

name: Space-grade connector supply
description: Connector and interconnect branch for high-reliability space electronics; supplier identity needs a separate audit before gating claims are promoted.

name: Vacuum-compatible compute harness
description: Harnessing, shielding, grounding, and thermal/mechanical interface branch for dense compute payloads. It becomes a bottleneck when high-current, high-speed interconnect, radiation tolerance, outgassing, and thermal paths all have to fit in a service-limited spacecraft package.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices vacuum-compatible harness design, shielded connectors, outgassing controls, grounding, or qualification for dense compute satellites.

name: Orbital compute ground segment integration
description: Ground software, gateway, customer API, billing, and operations integration needed to turn satellites into a usable compute service. This is a product bottleneck because the orbital hardware only becomes valuable when workloads, SLAs, billing, customer routing, and degraded-mode operations are integrated into a real service.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: Reviewed public sources do not price the ground software, gateway integration, customer API, billing, SLA monitoring, and operations stack needed for orbital compute service.

name: In-orbit serviceability and recovery strategy
description: Strategy for failed payload isolation, degraded-mode operation, software recovery, replacement launch, and disposal when physical service is limited. It is a bottleneck because a terrestrial data center can swap hardware, while an orbital data center must absorb failures through redundancy, software recovery, and replacement launches.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: No reviewed public source prices degraded-mode operation, failed-payload isolation, replacement launches, insurance, or disposal cost for orbital compute service.

name: Orbital compute business-model validation
description: Customer, latency, reliability, insurance, utilization, launch cost, and terrestrial competition assumptions that decide whether orbital compute becomes economic. This is the gating node for supplier and ticker exposure: without useful-kW, utilization, thermal throttling, lifetime, and replacement cadence, company leads are premature.

metrics.name: Cost disclosure
metrics.description: The proposal lacks reviewed useful-kW, utilization, payload lifetime, thermal throttling, insurance, and replacement-cadence data, so cost per useful compute kW cannot be audited yet.

name: Compute power per satellite
description: Useful compute kW per satellite after power, thermal, radiation, and duty-cycle limits. Public SpaceX system-level claims need review before values are used.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: Blocking commercial unknown: without a reviewed useful-kW value after solar power, eclipse duty cycle, thermal throttling, radiation derating, and network overhead, orbital compute economics cannot be priced.

name: Orbital network latency and bandwidth
description: Bandwidth and latency between compute satellites, Starlink links, gateways, and customers.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: Starlink optical-link sources support network technology context, but not audited orbital compute latency, bandwidth reservation, gateway capacity, or workload-level data movement cost.

name: Orbital thermal dissipation margin
description: Thermal margin after waste heat, radiator area, orbital heating, coating degradation, and throttling.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.currentValue: unknown - no reviewed useful heat-rejection margin
metrics.description: NASA thermal-control sources support the physics and technology categories, but not a reviewed heat-rejection budget for SpaceX orbital data-center payloads.

name: Launch cost per useful compute kW
description: Economic metric linking Starship/Falcon launch cost, payload lifetime, power generation, thermal throttling, utilization, and replacement cadence.

metrics.name: Current audited value
metrics.description: Blocking commercial unknown: this value must combine launch price, payload lifetime, utilization, power, and thermal throttling before the map can support paid exposure.

name: SpaceX
description: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. is the product owner/operator in both SpaceX-centered maps.
